Solicitation of research Proposals for new studies to be undertaken/sponsored under BPR&D Research 
Studies Programme (2026–27) 
  BPR&D invites research proposals from bona fide Universities, Institutions, Organizations, Departments, 
CAPFs, and CPOs for undertaking research studies on any of the topics listed below, with a focus on identified areas 
of contemporary relevance to policing and allied fields. The proposals should aim to generate meaningful, evidence-
based findings and practical recommendations that may contribute to improving policing practices, policy formulation, 
and the broader criminal justice system.  
2. The objectives outlined for each research topic are indicative and represent the minimum areas to be 
addressed. The researcher shall appropriately define and justify the universe/population, sample size, sampling 
methodology, and reference period in the research proposal, keeping in view the nature, scope, and objectives of 
the proposed study. The proposed methodology should be designed to ensure that the objectives of the study are 
effectively and comprehensively achieved. Researchers may also examine any other relevant or emerging aspects 
related to the identified research topic, wherever considered appropriate, to enhance the scope, relevance, and utility 
of the study.  
 
THEMES 
 
TOPICS 
 
I. NEW AGE 
POLICING, 
ARTIFICIAL 
INTELLEIGENCE 
& CYBER 
SECURITY  
 
1. New Age Policing in times of Social Media 
 To examine the evolving role of social media in crime prevention, investigation and 
public engagement. 
 To assess the use of social media intelligence and OSINT for policing and threat 
assessment. 
 To examine challenges arising from misinformation, disinformation, deepfakes and 
online mobilisation. 
 To assess police capabilities, skills and institutional mechanisms for social-media-
enabled policing. 
 To examine legal, ethical, privacy and human-rights considerations in social media 
policing. 
 To develop an evidence-based framework for responsible, technology-enabled and 
citizen-centric social media policing. 
 
2. Combating Digital Arrest Frauds in India: A Comprehensive Assessment of 
Modus Operandi, Victimisation, Police Response, Financial Investigation, Inter-
State Coordination and Prosecution 
 To examine the evolving modus operandi, techniques and criminal networks involved in 
digital arrest frauds. 
 To assess patterns of victimisation, financial losses, vulnerability factors and reporting 
behaviour. 
 To evaluate police response mechanisms, including complaint handling, investigation, 
cyber-forensics and victim support. 
 To examine challenges in financial investigation, tracing, freezing and recovery of fraud 
proceeds. 
 To assess inter-State coordination and institutional mechanisms for investigation and 
disruption of digital arrest networks. 
 To examine prosecution and evidentiary challenges and develop an integrated 
framework for prevention, investigation and prosecution of digital arrest frauds. 
 
3. AI and Advanced Data Analytics for Disrupting Narco-Trafficking Networks and 
Improving Police Response to the challenges of Misinformation and Deepfakes 
 To assess AI and advanced data analytics for identifying and disrupting narco-trafficking 
networks. 
 To examine multi-source data fusion, network analytics and predictive intelligence for 
detecting trafficking patterns. 
 To assess AI-enabled capabilities for detecting and verifying misinformation and 
deepfakes. 
 
Page 2 of 20 
 
 To identify police capabilities, infrastructure, skills and institutional requirements for AI-
enabled policing. 
 To examine legal, ethical, privacy, accuracy and evidentiary challenges associated with 
AI-based policing applications. 
 To develop an integrated framework for responsible AI adoption in narco-trafficking 
intelligence and for detection, verification and response to misinformation/deepfake 
response. 
 
4. Enhancing aviation security through AI-Driven behavioural threat detection at 
Indian airports 
 To assess existing behavioural threat detection and passenger-security practices at 
Indian airports. 
 To examine the potential of AI-enabled behavioural analytics as decision-support tool 
for early identification of security threats. 
 To assess the integration of AI-based detection with existing airport surveillance, 
screening and intelligence systems. 
 To identify challenges relating to accuracy, false positives, bias, privacy, data protection 
and human oversight. 
 To assess the technological, infrastructural, training and institutional requirements for 
AI-enabled aviation security. 
 To develop an evidence-based framework for responsible and effective deployment of 
AI-driven behavioural threat detection at Indian airports. 
 
5. Geospatial and Cross-Platform Social Media Intelligence for Public-Order 
Preparedness 
 To assess the use of geospatial and cross-platform social media intelligence for public-
order preparedness and situational awareness. 
 To identify emerging events, mobilisation patterns, misinformation and geographically 
concentrated risks through social media analytics. 
 To examine integration of social media intelligence with GIS, police control rooms, field 
intelligence and emergency-response systems. 
 To assess police capabilities, technological infrastructure and skills required for effective 
social media intelligence. 
 To examine legal, ethical, privacy and operational challenges in cross-platform 
intelligence gathering and analysis. 
 To develop an evidence-based framework for early warning, risk assessment and 
coordinated public-order preparedness. 
 
6. Cyber-Physical Security Convergence in Protecting Critical Industrial 
Infrastructures: Challenges and Best Practices for CAPFs 
 To assess emerging cyber-physical threats to critical industrial infrastructure. 
 To examine the convergence of cyber and physical security systems. 
 To assess CAPF capabilities for threat detection and incident response. 
 To identify gaps in technology, skills, training and inter-agency coordination. 
 To examine relevant national and international best practices. 
 To develop a capability framework for integrated cyber-physical security. 
 
II. INTERNAL 
SECURITY 
 
7. Operationalising PRAHAAR ( Prevention, Responses, Aggregating Internal 
Capacities, Human Rights & Rule of Law, Attenuating, Aligning & shaping and 
Recovery & Resilience): From National Counter Terrorism Strategy to State-Level 
Counter-Terrorism Capabilities 
 To assess the operationalization of the PRAHAAR framework at the State level. 
 To identify institutional, legal, intelligence and operational capability gaps. 
 To assess Central–State and inter-agency coordination mechanisms. 
 To examine preparedness for prevention, response, investigation and recovery. 
 To assess integration of human rights, rule of law and community resilience. 
 To develop measurable indicators and a State-level implementation framework. 
 
8. Demographic Change and Internal Security: Emerging Challenges for Policing 
and Governance in India 
 To examine demographic trends and their internal-security implications. 
 To assess the impact of urbanization, migration and population transitions on policing. 
 To examine implications for police deployment, infrastructure and manpower planning. 
 To assess community-policing and governance responses to demographic challenges. 
 To identify data and analytical requirements for evidence-based policing. 
 To develop a forward-looking policing and governance framework. 
 
 
Page 3 of 20 
 
9. Professional and Competency-Based Coastal Policing: Training, Career 
Incentives, and Marine Home Guards 
 To assess existing coastal-policing structures, training and manpower. 
 To identify competencies required for effective coastal and marine policing. 
 To assess gaps in specialized training and professional development. 
 To examine career incentives, progression and retention of coastal-policing personnel. 
 To assess the role of Marine Home Guards in coastal security. 
 To develop a competency-based framework for professional coastal policing. 
 
10. Future ready Border Guarding Forces: Integration of AI, drone and anti-drone 
technologies 
 To assess emerging border-security challenges and technology requirements. 
 To examine applications of AI, drones and anti-drone technologies. 
 To assess integration with existing surveillance and command systems. 
 To identify gaps in technology, infrastructure, cybersecurity and interoperability. 
 To assess training and skill requirements for technology-enabled border guarding. 
 To develop a technology-integration framework for future-ready border forces. 
 
11. Emerging Trends in cross – border narcotics and arms smuggling 
 To examine emerging routes, methods and networks involved in cross-border 
smuggling. 
 To assess the role of drones, digital platforms and emerging technologies. 
 To analyze linkages between narcotics, arms smuggling and organized crime. 
 To assess vulnerabilities in land, coastal and air-border routes. 
 To examine intelligence-sharing and inter-agency coordination mechanisms. 
 To develop an intelligence-led framework for prevention and disruption of trafficking 
networks. 
 
12. Comprehensive Study of Vibrant Villages Programme: Integrating Local 
Economic Development, Youth Engagement and Community Policing for 
Strengthening Community Resilience and Border Security 
 To assess VVP implementation in border villages. 
 To examine linkages between local development, livelihoods and border security. 
 To assess youth engagement and community-resilience initiatives. 
 To examine the role of community policing in strengthening border communities. 
 To assess coordination among local communities, administration, police and CAPFs. 
 To develop an integrated framework linking development, youth engagement, 
community policing and border security. 
 
III. CRIME 
AND 
INVESTIGATION 
 
13. Narco-trafficking and Organized Crime: Mapping Networks, Finances, and 
Criminal Ecosystems 
 To examine the structure and evolution of narco-trafficking networks. 
 To map key actors, linkages and criminal ecosystems. 
 To analyse financial flows, money laundering and asset concealment. 
 To assess the role of digital platforms and emerging technologies. 
 To examine intelligence, investigation and inter-agency coordination mechanisms. 
 To develop a framework for network disruption and financial investigation. 
 
14. Strengthening Criminal Justice Response to Victims of Human Trafficking from 
Rescue to Reintegration  
 To assess the response to victims from identification and rescue to reintegration. 
 To examine mechanisms for victim protection, support and legal assistance. 
 To assess coordination among police, prosecution, government and civil-society 
agencies. 
 To identify investigation and prosecution challenges. 
 To assess rehabilitation, compensation and reintegration mechanisms. 
 To develop a victim-centric framework for sustainable rehabilitation and reintegration. 
15. Open-Source Data Fusion and Multi-Source Link Analysis for Advanced 
Investigative Intelligence 
 To assess the use of OSINT and data fusion in criminal investigations. 
 To identify relevant open-source and legally accessible data sources. 
 To examine techniques for entity, relationship and network analysis. 
 To assess the reliability and evidentiary value of open-source intelligence. 
 To identify legal, ethical, privacy and operational challenges. 
 To develop an operational framework for multi-source investigative intelligence. 
 
 
Page 4 of 20 
 
16. Inter-State Cybercrime Networks: Challenges in Jurisdiction, Coordination and 
Digital Investigation 
 To examine the structure and modus operandi of inter-State cybercrime networks. 
 To identify jurisdictional and procedural challenges in investigation. 
 To assess inter-State and inter-agency coordination mechanisms. 
 To examine challenges in digital evidence collection and forensic investigation. 
 To assess mechanisms for financial tracing, account freezing and recovery. 
 To develop a framework for coordinated inter-State cybercrime investigation. 
 
17. Cybercrime-as-a-Service in India: Emerging Criminal Ecosystems and Policing 
Challenges 
 To examine the evolution and structure of Cybercrime-as-a-Service ecosystems. 
 To identify key actors, services and operational linkages. 
 To assess the role of digital platforms, encryption and cryptocurrencies. 
 To identify challenges in attribution, investigation and disruption. 
 To assess the role of digital forensics, financial investigation and network analysis. 
 To develop a framework for disrupting cybercrime service ecosystems. 
 
18. Forensic Capabilities as Force Multipliers in Criminal Investigation: Assessment 
of Their Impact on Investigation Quality, Timeliness and Trial Outcomes in 
Heinous Offences 
 To assess forensic capabilities in the investigation of heinous offences. 
 To examine their impact on investigation quality and evidence gathering. 
 To assess the effect of forensic processes on investigation timelines. 
 To examine the contribution of forensic evidence to prosecution and trial outcomes. 
 To identify gaps in forensic infrastructure, manpower, technology and quality assurance. 
 To develop indicators and recommendations for strengthening forensic capabilities. 
 
IV. CAPACITY 
BUILDING 
 
19. Towards an Evidence-Based Framework for Core Police Training in India: 
Assessment of Training Needs, Competencies, Methodologies, Outcomes and 
Transfer to Field Performance 
 To assess training needs across police ranks and functional roles. 
 To identify core competencies required for contemporary policing. 
 To evaluate existing curricula, methodologies and assessment practices. 
 To assess training outcomes and transfer of learning to field performance. 
 To identify institutional and operational gaps affecting training effectiveness. 
 To develop an evidence-based framework for outcome-oriented police training. 
 
20. Study on Faculty Development Courses being conducted across 351 Police 
Training Institutions and their standardisation. 
 To map and assess faculty development programmes across 351 institutions. 
 To identify core competencies required for effective police trainers. 
 To assess variations in curricula, methodologies and assessment mechanisms. 
 To evaluate the effectiveness and outcomes of existing programmes. 
 To identify gaps and areas requiring standardization. 
 To develop a standardized framework for trainer development and certification. 
 
V. PUBLIC 
ORDER 
 
21. Transforming Beat Policing in India: Citizen-Centric, Rights-Based, and 
Constitutional Policing 
 To assess the current structure and functioning of beat policing. 
 To identify gaps in citizen engagement, accessibility and service delivery. 
 To examine the integration of rights-based and constitutional policing principles. 
 To assess the use of technology and local intelligence in beat policing. 
 To identify training, manpower and organizational requirements. 
 To develop a citizen-centric and rights-based model of beat policing. 
 
22. Night-Time Policing in Indian Cities: Deployment, Vulnerability and Service-
Delivery Gaps 
 To assess existing night-time police deployment and operational practices. 
 To identify crime, safety and vulnerability patterns during night hours. 
 To examine gaps in emergency response and essential police service delivery. 
 To assess deployment adequacy in relation to population, geography and risk. 
 To examine safety concerns affecting vulnerable groups during night hours. 
 To develop a risk-based framework for effective night-time policing. 
 
 
 
Page 5 of 20 
 
23. Crowd Management to Crowd Safety: Risk-Based Planning, and Organiser 
Accountability 
 To assess existing approaches to crowd management and public-event security. 
 To identify crowd-related risks and factors contributing to escalation. 
 To examine risk-based planning, preparedness and emergency response mechanisms. 
 To assess the role and accountability of event organisers and other stakeholders. 
 To identify gaps in police training, technology and inter-agency coordination. 
 To develop a crowd-safety framework based on prevention, preparedness and 
proportionate response. 
 
24. Financial Signatures of Organised Public Disorder: Role of Financial Investigation 
in Identifying Coordinated Criminal Activity  
 To examine financial patterns associated with organised public disorder. 
 To identify financial linkages, funding channels and suspicious transactions. 
 To assess the role of financial investigation in identifying coordinated criminal activity. 
 To examine mechanisms for tracing illicit funds and associated assets. 
 To assess coordination among police, financial-intelligence and enforcement agencies. 
 To develop a framework for integrating financial intelligence into public-order 
investigations. 
 
25. Close Coast/internal water patrol – Study Global Best Practices 
 To examine global models of coastal and inland-waterway policing. 
 To assess patrol structures, vessels, surveillance systems and operational practices. 
 To examine training and competency requirements for strengthening operational 
capabilities for water-based policing. 
 To assess coordination among police, maritime and other security agencies. 
 To identify practices adaptable to India’s coastal and inland-water environments. 
 To develop a framework for strengthening water-based patrol capabilities in India. 
 
VI. MODUS 
OPENRANDI 
 
26. Emerging Trends in the Modus Operandi of Crime in India: Possible use of AI and 
Data Analytics an Integrated Assessment of Criminal Methods, Investigation, 
Intelligence, Prosecution, and Preventive Strategies 
 To identify emerging trends and changes in criminal modus operandi. 
 To assess the use of AI, digital technologies and data analytics by criminals. 
 To examine implications for police intelligence and investigation. 
 To assess emerging requirements in evidence collection, forensics and prosecution. 
 To identify technology, skills and institutional gaps in crime prevention and detection. 
 To develop an integrated framework for intelligence-led and technology-enabled policing. 
 
VII. CRIMINAL 
JUSTICE 
 
27. Transforming Criminal Justice in India: A Comprehensive Study on the impact of 
New Criminal Laws on Criminal Investigation, Prosecution, Judicial Proceedings, 
Victim and Witness Protection, Forensic Practices, and Prison Administration 
 To assess the impact of new criminal laws on police investigation and procedures. 
 To examine their implications for prosecution and judicial proceedings. 
 To assess changes in victim and witness protection mechanisms. 
 To examine implications for forensic investigation and evidence management. 
 To assess implementation challenges across police, prosecution, courts and prisons. 
 To develop recommendations for effective institutional implementation of the new 
criminal laws. 
VIII. WOMEN & 
CHILDREN 
28. The study of conviction rate in rape and POCSO Act cases: Identifying Gaps in 
Investigation & Prosecution and Strategies to Increase Conviction Rate  
 To analyse conviction patterns and case outcomes in rape and POCSO cases. 
 To identify investigation-related gaps affecting case outcomes. 
 To examine prosecution, evidentiary and procedural challenges. 
 To assess delays in investigation, forensic examination and trial. 
 To identify good practices associated with effective investigation and prosecution. 
 To develop strategies for strengthening investigation and prosecution outcomes. 
 
29. Large pendency of court cases relating to Crime Against Women and Children: 
Identifying Systemic Gaps and Delays in Justice Delivery and its impact on the 
Criminal Justice System  
 To assess the extent and patterns of pendency in cases involving women and children. 
 To identify systemic and procedural causes of delay. 
 To examine bottlenecks across investigation, prosecution and judicial proceedings. 
 To assess the impact of prolonged proceedings on victims, witnesses and the justice 
system. 
 To examine institutional capacity and coordination gaps. 
 To develop measures for reducing pendency and improving timely justice delivery. 
 
Page 6 of 20 
 
IX. CORRECTIONAL 
ADMINISTRATION 
30. Undertrial Detention and Prison Overcrowding in India: A Comprehensive 
Assessment of Systemic Challenges, Reform Options and Alternatives to 
Incarceration 
 To assess the scale and causes of undertrial detention and prison overcrowding. 
 To examine systemic factors contributing to prolonged pre-trial detention. for 
strengthening responsible domestic manufacturing capabilities under an appropriate 
 To assess the impact of overcrowding on prison administration and prisoner welfare. 
 To examine bail, legal-aid and case-management mechanisms. 
 To assess alternatives to incarceration and their applicability. 
 To develop evidence-based options for reducing unnecessary detention and 
overcrowding. 
 
31. National Study on Sentence Planning in Prisons: Individualised Planning from 
Admission to Community Reintegration 
 To assess existing sentence-planning practices across Indian prisons. 
 To examine individual assessment of prisoners’ risks, needs and rehabilitation 
requirements. 
 To assess integration of education, treatment, skills and behavioural interventions into 
sentence plans. 
 To examine monitoring and review mechanisms during incarceration. 
 To assess linkage between sentence planning and post-release reintegration. 
 To develop a standardized, individualized sentence-planning framework. 
 
32. Digital Transformation of Prisons in India: A Study of E-Prisons System and its 
impact on Prison Management, Technological Gaps, Institutional Challenges, and 
Opportunities for Reform 
 To assess the implementation and utilization of the E-Prisons system. 
 To examine its impact on prison administration, information management and service 
delivery. 
 To identify technological, infrastructure and interoperability gaps. 
 To assess challenges in digital governance, cybersecurity and data management. 
 To identify opportunities for AI, analytics and technology-enabled correctional services. 
 To develop a framework for effective digital transformation of prison administration. 
 
33. Perceptions of Prison Officers about their Role in the Correctional Administration 
Continuum: Balancing Prison Safety and Security with Rehabilitation and Social 
Re-entry 
 To examine prison officers’ perceptions of their roles and responsibilities. 
 To assess the balance between security, discipline and rehabilitation functions. 
 To identify factors influencing officers’ approach to correctional administration. 
 To assess training, organisational support and professional development needs. 
 To examine challenges in facilitating rehabilitation and social reintegration. 
 To develop measures for strengthening the professional role of prison officers. 
 
34. An analytical study of Remission Policies and Premature Release 
 To examine remission and premature-release policies across States and jurisdictions. 
 To assess variations in eligibility criteria, procedures and decision-making mechanisms. 
 To examine institutional, legal and administrative challenges in implementation. 
 To assess transparency, consistency and review mechanisms in release decisions. 
 To examine post-release supervision and reintegration arrangements. 
 To develop evidence-based recommendations for a consistent and effective remission 
framework. 
 
35. Mental Health Management and De-addiction in Indian Prisons: Challenges, and 
Interventions 
 To assess the prevalence and nature of mental-health and substance-use concerns in 
prisons. 
 To evaluate existing screening, treatment and de-addiction services. 
 To identify gaps in trained personnel, infrastructure and continuity of care. 
 To assess rehabilitation and psychosocial-support interventions. 
 To examine linkages between prison-based treatment and community services after 
release. 
 To develop an integrated framework for prison mental-health management and de-
addiction. 
 
36. High-Security Prisons in India: Balancing Institutional Security and Effective 
Correctional Administration 
 To assess the structure and functioning of high-security prisons. 
 
Page 7 of 20 
 
 To examine security risks, classification systems and management practices. 
 To assess the balance between institutional security and correctional objectives. 
 To identify gaps in infrastructure, technology, staffing and specialised training. 
 To examine rehabilitation and correctional interventions suitable for high-risk prisoners. 
 To develop a framework for secure, effective and correctionally oriented high-security 
prisons. 
 
37. Open Correctional Institutions: From Custodial Care to Community-Based 
Rehabilitation and Reintegration  
 To examine the structure and functioning of open correctional institutions in India. 
 To assess their contribution to rehabilitation, responsibility and community reintegration. 
 To examine eligibility, classification and risk-management mechanisms. 
 To assess employment, education, family contact and community-based interventions. 
 To identify operational and institutional challenges affecting effectiveness. 
 To develop a framework for expanding and strengthening open correctional practices. 
 
38. Impact Assessment of Skill Development and Post-Release Employment among 
Prisoners in India 
 To assess skill-development programmes available to prisoners. 
 To examine their relevance to labour-market and local employment opportunities. 
 To assess post-release employment, livelihood and income outcomes. 
 To identify barriers to employment and economic reintegration after release. 
 To examine employer, industry and government partnerships supporting prisoner 
employment. 
 To develop an outcome-oriented framework linking prison skills training with sustainable 
employment. 
 
39. Recidivism Prevention among Young Adult Offenders (18–21 Years) in India: 
Development of an Evidence-Based, Individualized and Community-Integrated 
Rehabilitation Model 
 To examine the patterns and factors associated with recidivism among young adult 
offenders. 
 To assess individual, family, peer, educational and socio-economic risk factors. 
 To evaluate existing rehabilitation and behavioural interventions. 
 To assess the role of education, skills, employment and community support in preventing 
reoffending. 
 To examine post-release supervision and reintegration mechanisms. 
 To develop an individualized and community-integrated rehabilitation model for young 
adults. 
 
40. Emerging Dimensions of Juvenile Delinquency in India: Cyber Offending, 
Organised Crime, Substance Abuse and Peer Networks—Implications for 
Preventive Policing  
 To examine emerging patterns of juvenile delinquency, including cyber offending and 
substance abuse. 
 To assess the influence of peer networks, organised crime and digital environments. 
 To identify risk and protective factors associated with juvenile offending. 
 To assess existing preventive-policing and community interventions. 
 To examine rehabilitation, diversion and family-support mechanisms. 
 To develop evidence-based strategies for prevention and early intervention. 
 
X. TRANSPORT 
& MOBILITY 
 
41. Role Allocation between RPF and GRP: Identifying and Mitigating Gaps and 
Overlaps in Rail Security 
 To examine the existing roles and responsibilities of RPF and GRP in railway security. 
 To identify functional overlaps, gaps and jurisdictional ambiguities. 
 To assess coordination in crime prevention, investigation and passenger security. 
 To examine information-sharing, command-and-control and joint-response mechanisms. 
 To identify manpower, training and technological capability gaps. 
 To develop a clearer framework for role allocation and coordinated railway security. 
 
XI. ROAD 
SAFETY 42. Scientific Investigation of Fatal Road Crashes: Developing a Standardised Police 
Protocol for Evidence Collection, Accident Reconstruction and Prosecution.  
 To assess existing police procedures for investigation of fatal road crashes. 
 To identify gaps in crime-scene evidence collection and documentation. 
 To examine the use of accident reconstruction, forensic and digital evidence. 
 To assess investigative standards for determining causation and liability. 
 To identify training, technology and inter-agency coordination requirements. 
 
Page 8 of 20 
 
 To develop a standardised police protocol for scientific crash investigation and 
prosecution. 
 
43.  Effectiveness of ITMS on Pedestrian Safety in Cities 
 To examine the protocols and criteria adopted for deployment of red-light cameras, speed 
cameras, and alcohol detection systems for pedestrian safety. 
 To assess the effectiveness of these ITMS interventions in reducing pedestrian fatalities 
and serious injuries. 
 To analyse changes in pedestrian fatalities and crashes following the deployment of red-
light cameras, speed cameras, and alcohol detection systems. 
 To identify high-risk locations and assess the role of ITMS in addressing pedestrian safety

BPR&D’S GUIDELINE FOR DRAFTING RESEARCH PROPOSAL 
1. The Title of Project 
3. Aim of the Project: 
The broad aim of the project emphasizing the overall thrust of the proposed investigation should be 
clearly mentioned. 
3. Statement of the Problem 
In the opening paragraphs of the research proposal, the problem to be investigated should be stated 
clearly and briefly. The key questions and the location of the problem in the theoretical context of the 
concerned discipline should be specified. The significance of the problem, the contribution which the 
proposed study is expected to make to theory and methodology as well as its practical importance, and 
national relevance should be specifically indicated. 
4. Overview of Literature 
Summarizing the current status of research in the area, including major findings, the project proposal 
should clearly demonstrate the relevance or insufficiency of the findings or approaches for the 
investigation of the problem at hand. 
5. The Conceptual Framework 
Given the problem and the theoretical perspective for investigating the problem, the proposal should 
clearly indicate the concepts to be used and demonstrate their relevance for the study. It should further 
specify the dimensions of empirical reality that need to be explored for investigating the problem. 
6. Research Questions or Objectives or Hypotheses 
Given the conceptual framework and the specification of dimensions, the specific question to be 
answered through the proposed research should be sharply formulated. In the case of an explanatory 
research design, specification of variables and posting of relationship among them through specific 
hypotheses must form a part of the research proposal. 
7. Research Methodology 
7.1. Coverage 
If in the light of the questions raised or the hypotheses proposed to be tested, sampling becomes 
necessary, full information on the following points should be given: 
1. Universe of study 
2. Sampling frame 
3. Sampling procedure 
4. Units of observation and sample size 
[If the study requires any control groups, these should be specifically mentioned. An explanation of the 
determination of size and type of sample will also be necessary. Proposals not requiring a sample 
selection should specify their strategy appropriately and describe the rationale.] 
7.2. Data Collection 
The different type of data that are proposed to be gathered should be specifically mentioned. The 
sources for each type of data and the tools and techniques that will be used for collection of different 
type of data should be specified. 
 For questionnaire or schedule to be used the following should be indicated: 
(i) Distribution of questionnaire of schedule in different sections, e.g. Identification data, socio-
economic data, questions on various sub-themes. 
(ii) Approximate number of questions to be asked from each respondent. 
(iii) Any scaling techniques to be included in the instrument. 
(iv) Any projective tests incorporated to the questionnaire/schedule. 
(v) Approximate time needed per interview. 
 
Page 17 of 20 
 
(vi) Any plans for index-construction. 
(vii) Coding plan (whether the questions and responses will be pre-coded or not; whether the coding 
is done for computer or for hand tabulation). 
 For interviews, the following details should be given: 
(i) How they are to be conducted (free associational, non-directive, focused, direct or on 
telephone). 
(ii) Particular characteristics that interviews must have. 
For the use of observation techniques, describe: 
(i) The type of observation: participant, quasi-participant, non-participant;

NOTIFICATION

Subject: Policy/Guideline for CUSB vehicle sticker.

४

Vehicle stickers are properties of the CUSB and are liable to be withdrawn/ cancelled at
any moment without assigning any reason.

. All vehicles entering the campus be required to obtain Entry Slip (for one time entry) or

permanent pass i.e. vehicle sticker.

डे Validity of a sticker for a regular employee shall be for 02 academic years and for a

contractual employee one academic year. For this purpose, an academic year shall be
considered from 04 July to 30 June. A sticker issued during any time in an academic
year shall expire at the end of applicable academic year. Moreover, the sticker’s validity
shall expire with termination of an employee’s services to CUSB and /completion of
academic programme for a student/research:scholar.

General terms and conditions:  
 
1 How to apply Candidates who fulfill the criterion to fill up the ONLINE APPLICATION 
format by clicking on the following link……..   
2 Number of posts Director, CCMB reserves the right to increase/decrease the number of 
positions and also cancel the recruitment process for the positions 
mentioned above at any stage of the recruitment process.  The decision 
of the Director, CSIR-CCMB will be final and binding. 
3 Age relaxation Age relaxation as per CSIR/Govt. of India gui delines.  Age will be 
calculated as on the last date of receipt of online applications. 
4 Awaiting result/ 
Pursuing degree 
Those candidates who are still pursuing/ awaiting result for their degree 
M.Sc./ B.Tech./ PhD or any other qualification for the above post(s) as 
on the date of application will not be considered.  
5 Eligibility criterion Candidate should note that non -fulfillment of the eligibility criterion will 
result in cancellation of candidature at any stage 
6 Experience The period of experience in a discipline / area of work, wherever 
prescribed, shall be counted after the date of acquiring the minimum 
prescribed educational qualifications prescribed for that post. 
7 Screening of 
applications 
The applicants will be subjected to short listing by CCMB 
scientists/designated committee according to the current requirement 
and the candidate’s shortlisted for interview will be displayed on CCMB 
website. 
8 Selection procedure The candidate(s) shortlisted by CCMB scientists/designated committee 
have to appear for interview in person/online before  the Selection 
Committee.  The  date, time and venue of the test/interview will be 
notified in due course through email only. 
 
9 Result / Panel for 
waitlisted candidate 
Based upon the performance of candidates in the interview, result of 
selected candidates against the number of post available in the project 
for each post code, will be declared and posted on CCMB website.  A 
panel of waitlisted candidates in order of merit will also be formed for 
each post code, which will be valid for one year.  The panel may be 
operated on the recommendation of Project Investigator for meeting out 
any future requirement in the project arises due to resignation of 
incumbent/ non -joining of selected candidates/ further 
unforeseen/urgent requirement of project manpower for the same 
position in same project. 
10 Engagement The engagement shall be initial ly for a short duration based on 
availability of funds  which may be extended or curtailed based on the 
conduct and the performance of the incumbent as well as requirement 
of the institute.  However, the engagement will not be beyond the tenure 
of the proje ct and shall expire automatically on the expiry of project 
tenure, in which candidate has been selected.  The engagement under 
projects does not confer any right/claim whatsoever, either explicitly or 
implicitly on the appointee for regular appointment in CSIR/CCMB, 
against any post or otherwise under any legal conditions or precedent. 
The engagement of project staff in different projects either in same 
Lab/Instt. or different Lab.Instt. of CSIR taken together shall not exceed 
5 years in any case.  
11 Leave The incumbent would not be entitled to any kind of regular leave. 
However, they would be allowed for one-day Leave for each completed 
month. 
12 TA/DA No TA/ DA admissible for attending test/interview, joining the position. 
13 Office timings/ Working 
hours 
The incumbent is  required to  perform the assigned duties during 
working hours i.e. from 9:30 AM to 6:00 PM on working days. The 
incumbent will not be allowed to take up any  other assignment during 
the period of engagement. He /She may be required to  work on  
Saturday/Sunday/other Gazetted holidays and beyond working hours 
also if need be. 
14 Tax deduction at source The Income Tax or any other tax liable to be deducted, as per the 
prevailing rules will be  deducted at source before effecting the 
payment. 
15 Confidentiality of data 
and documents 
The Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) of the data collected as well as 
the deliverables produced for the office shall remain with this office. 
No one shall utilize or publish or disclose or part with, to a third party, 
any part of the data or statistics or proceedings or information collected 
for the purpose of this assignment or during the course of assignment 
for the office,  without the express  written consent of the office.  The 
incumbent shall be bound to hand over the entire set of records of 
assignment to the Office before the expiry of the contract, and before 
the final payment is released by the office. 
16 Termination of Service The performance of project personnel would be reviewed periodically 
so that candidates not found up to the mark, could be terminated.  The 
engagement may be terminated at any time by the office without  
assigning any reasons by giving a one month notice. In case, the person 
desires to leave the assignment, he/s he may also do so by giving one 
month notice or payment of one month stipend in lieu of, which can be 
condoned/ curtailed/ extended depending upon the discretion  of the 
Competent Authority. 
17 DISCLAIMER Candidates who are applying for any of the above post shall ensure that 
they fulfill the essential qualifications.  If they apply without fulfilling the 
essential qualifications then it will be considered that they are giving 
wrong/misleading information.  The ONUS OF THIS ACTION WILL BE 
 
ON THE CANDIDATE and not on the Institute.  In case they are found 
not fulfilling the essential criteria or that they have provided misleading 
information, then their candidature for the post may be rejected at any 
stage of selection or after selection. 
18 Disqualification Canvassing in any form and / or bringing any influence political or 
otherwise will be treated as a disqualification for the post.
